subject: Critical Thinking
title: Modus Tollens: Reasoning Backward
description: One-minute skill: Modus Tollens: Reasoning Backward.

hook.text: If it rained, the street would be wet. The street is dry. Therefore it didn't rain. Equally flawless.

buildup.text: Modus tollens: If P then Q. Q is false. Therefore P is false. It's deduction in reverse.

discovery.text: Scientists use this constantly: if my theory is true, X should happen. X didn't happen. Theory is wrong.

twist.text: Karl Popper built his entire philosophy of science on modus tollens — falsification over confirmation.

climax.text: You can never prove a theory true, but modus tollens lets you prove one false with a single observation.

punchline.text: One black swan disproves 'all swans are white.'

quiz.question: What does modus tollens allow you to conclude?
options: If Q is true, P must be true
If Q is false, P must be false
If P is false, Q is false

details.summary: Modus tollens reasons backward from a denied consequence: if P then Q; Q is false; therefore P is false. It is the logical foundation of falsification, the engine that drives scientific progress by eliminating hypotheses.
details.whyItMatters: Modus tollens is how science rules out hypotheses—if a prediction fails, the theory behind it is in trouble.
takeaways: Denying the consequence validly denies the antecedent
It is the logical basis of scientific falsification
Denying the antecedent is its common invalid cousin

faq.question: How does modus tollens work in scientific reasoning?
faq.answer: If a theory predicts X but X does not occur, the theory is disconfirmed. This is how failed experiments eliminate hypotheses and drive scientific progress.

faq.question: What is the difference between modus tollens and denying the antecedent?
faq.answer: Modus tollens validly denies the antecedent from a denied consequent. Denying the antecedent (P is false, therefore Q is false) is a fallacy because Q may have other causes.
